html:
The forced removal by Britain of the French speaking Acadians from their farms in Nova Scotia and nearby lands, from 1755 to 1764. Of perhaps 14,000 Acadians, about 11,500 were deported.

Acadia had been French until 1713, when Britain took the peninsula. The Acadians lived under British rule for decades but refused an unconditional oath of loyalty that might force them to fight France. When the war that became the Seven Years' War began in North America, British officials and the governor of Massachusetts decided to remove them. Soldiers burned villages and loaded families on ships, often splitting them apart.

The deportees were scattered among the British colonies along the Atlantic, sent to England, and later to France. Thousands died of disease and shipwreck. Over the following years many found their way to Spanish Louisiana, where their descendants became the Cajuns. Others returned to the Maritimes later. Longfellow's poem Evangeline (1847) made the story famous.
sum: The forced removal by Britain of the French speaking Acadians from their farms in Nova Scotia and nearby lands, from 1755 to 1764. Of perhaps 14,000 Acadians, about 11,500 were deported.
